newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan activists protest over political reforms.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan activists protest over political reforms.

text.p: More than 1,000 people marched through the streets of Taipei on Sunday to protest about constitutional reforms in Taiwan.
The demonstrators carried placards demanding that they be given the right to hold plebiscites on matters of public concern.
Such issues as whether Taiwan should build a nuclear power station or state its independence from mainland China should be determined by popular vote, they said.
"We hope plebiscites can be included in the constitution," organiser and adviser to the main opposition Democratic Progressive Party Lin Yi-hsiung told reporters.
"A democracy's citizens should have their say on major public issues. This is our basic right," Lin said.

The National Assembly, an increasingly marginalised elected body whose sole function is to revise the constitution, has been reviewing a package of amendments proposed by the ruling Nationalist and opposition parties.
The Nationalist Party, which dominates the assembly's membership, has refused to discuss the plebiscite issue in debates about the constitution.
Lin's Democratic Progressive Party have supported the idea of holding plebiscites, but media reports say the opposition party may alter its position in return for Nationalist support on other issues.
Negotiations over the proposals are continuing.
Many critics have said constitutional amendments proposed by the Nationalists would create a strong executive presidency.
Under the proposals, the president would no longer need parliament's consent to appoint the premier and would have the power to dissolve parliament when he deems necesssary.
They would make explicit the president's powers to dictate policy on defence, foreign affairs, China and other national security issues. These powers are not currently defined in the constitution.
Parliament has no power to unseat the president or vice president, who since March 1996 have been elected by popular vote.
The amendments would require the votes of three-fifths of deputies to impeach the chief executive and a two-thirds vote to sack him.
